narrative:
The model estimated your probability of bad credit at 35%, meaning about a one-in-three chance that you would struggle to repay as agreed. That was above the bank’s approval cutoff for this loan, so your application was denied even though 35% is below an even chance.

The leading reason was your checking-account status: a balance in the 0–200 DM range was the strongest factor pushing toward bad credit. This band is much less common among approved applicants than having no checking account, and it signaled weaker day-to-day liquidity. Your credit history was the second most important factor and worked in your favor, reducing estimated risk; critical/other credits appear for about one third of approved applicants, so this category was not the main warning sign. The third factor, the amount requested—3,617 DM versus an approved average of about 3,020 DM—also leaned toward good credit rather than driving the denial. In short, the account-balance signal and other smaller risk factors outweighed the favorable credit-history and amount signals.

To improve your chances, ask the lender whether a manual review or lower-risk product is possible, focus on raising your checking balance and avoiding overdrafts, and strengthen your credit record by paying existing obligations on time. Consider reapplying after those changes, or adding a guarantor if the lender allows it.
